seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Many thanks for book of verses . Hope you got the German version of my play. As there is nothing to be hoped for from Mr Quinn I wrote urgently to my agent Mr Pinker, Talbot House, Arundel Street, Strand, asking him to cable Huebsch for an advance of royalties on any or all my books. Could you perhaps telephone to him, Mr Pinker, to ask if he has received my letter . It is now I want the reply not later on. I am sorry to note that you and your friends are also in bad circumstances. I can get on fairly well after New Year. The meantime is the difficulty. Will you please send me the last number of the Little Review. Thanks.

div.note: Presumably Pound’s Quia Pauper Amavi, published in October 1919 by the Egoist Press in London in an edition of 500 copies, with a special edition of 110 copies printed on hand-made paper (Donald Gallup, Ezra Pound: A Bibliography [Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 1983], 27-28). The volume contained, among other poems, Pound’s recent translations of Provençal poetry, a version of his “Three Cantos,” and his controversial translation, Homage to Sextus Propertius, “a thoroughly modern, Vorticist ‘portrait’; the refraction of the ancient poet through a modern intelligence, or the superimposition of the one upon the other” (A. David Moody, Ezra Pound: Poet, A Portrait of the Man and his Work, vol. 1 [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007], 350).

JJ’s play Exiles was translated into German by Hannah von Mettal as Verbannte: Schauspiel in drei Akten (Zurich: Rascher & Cie, 1919). It was published, according to JJ, on 1 April 1919 (see JJ to Pound, 1 April 1919, notes).

The New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924), a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, had purchased a number of items from JJ and had agreed to buy his Ulysses manuscript. After delays, on 5 February 1920 Quinn cabled JJ an advance of 3,000 lire or $153.85, and on 15 August 1920 another advance of 3,400 francs or $250, with an additional payment of 1,400 francs in the fall of 1920 (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 237, 241-42, 245-46, 254, 258). For a full account, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

JJ had written his London literary agent J.B. Pinker (prob. 1862 or 1863-1922) on 7 November 1919 (LI 130). Once informed of JJ’s plight, his American publisher B.W Huebsch (1876-1964) sent royalties. JJ wrote Pinker on 7 December 1919 to thank him for “cheque remitted and kindly thank also Mr Huebsch for his prompt reply” (LII 456).
Pound replied to JJ on 24 November 1919: “Pinker answers my phone call to the effect that he has answered your letter by express letter” (Pound/Joyce 161).

In January 1920, JJ was to begin receiving a five-percent interest income on £5,000 in war loan securities, settled on him by an anonymous donor who later revealed herself to be Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961). For a full account, see JJ to Pound, 24 October 1919, notes.

The “Cyclops” episode of Ulysses appeared in four numbers of The Little Review, vol. 6, nos. 7-10 (November, December 1919; January, March 1920): 38-54, 50-60, 53-61, 54-60. See JJ to Pound, 24 October 1919, notes. If JJ means the October 1919 number, that issue did not contain anything from Ulysses, but printed material by Sherwood Anderson, William Carlos Williams, Dorothy Richardson, and others, as well as a portion of the serialized essay, “The Chinese Written Character as a Medium for Poetry,” by Pound and Ernest Fenollosa (57-64). As Pound had ceased acting as foreign editor of The Little Review – a role taken up by John Rodker and Jules Romains – he was no longer able to send JJ copies of the magazine regularly.
